ABSTRACT  
Lipases are versatile catalysts that hydrolyze ester bonds of water-insoluble glycerides 
or carry out reversible reactions at the water/lipid interface. The remarkable 
characteristics of lipases from the genus Rhizopus are their high sn-1,3-positional 
specificity, enantioselectivity and activity in nonaqueous media, which make them 
one of the most desirable enzymes for many applications, including lipid modification 
and biodiesel and chiral organic compound synthesis. sn-1,3-position-specific 
Rhizopus lipases are particularly useful for the production of structured 
triacylglycerols. Significant progress has been made regarding lipases from the genus 
Rhizopus, including gene sequencing, elucidation of the protein structure and catalytic 
function, heterologous expression and redesigning Rhizopus lipases for valuable 
properties, which is receiving increasing academic and industrial attention. In this 
review, we present a comprehensive overview of Rhizopus lipases, focusing on (a) the 
characteristics of Rhizopus lipases, (b) Rhizopus lipase genes and structural features, 
(c) strategies for heterologous expression of Rhizopus lipase genes in yeast system, (d) 
progress in protein engineering for the improvement of the properties of Rhizopus 
lipases, and (e) development of biotechnological applications.  
 
 
Keywords: lipase; Rhizopus species; characterization; heterologous expression; 
bioengineering; biodiesel; enantioselectivity; sn-1,3-position specificity

1. Introduction  
  Lipases (triacylglycerol acyl hydrolases, EC 3.1.1.3) are a class of enzymes that 
catalyze the hydrolysis of fats at the water/lipid interface in aqueous media, while in 
non-aqueous media, the biochemical reactions driven by lipases include hydrolysis, 
interesterification, alcoholysis, acidolysis and esterification [1]. Furthermore, lipases 
have chemo-, region- and stereo-selective properties, which make lipases one of the 
most desirable enzymes for many industries. Lipases are the third largest group of 
industrial enzymes after proteases and amylases [2] and are extensively used in many 
industries, such as foods, flavors, detergents, pharmaceuticals, bioenergy and fine 
chemicals [3]. 
  Lipases exist widely in nature, including in yeasts, fungi, bacteria, animals and 
plants. Fungal lipases are preferentially applied industrially due to their high stability 
and wide substrate specificity. Rhizopus sp., which is classified in the family 
Mucoraceae in the order Mucorales of the phylum Zygomycota, are recognized as one 
of the best sources for the production of lipases [4]. Based on the morphological 
taxonomy developed by Schipper, Rhizopus sp. have been reclassified into three 
groups: the Rhizopus oryzae group, the R. microspores group and the R. stolonifer 
group [5]. Despite some minor variations, Rhizopus isolates, such as R. arrhizus, R. 
delemar and R. javanicus, have been combined into the same species, R. oryzae [5]. 
The recently developed classification based on molecular taxonomy indicates that R. 
oryzae can be divided into R. oryzae and R. delemar [6] and that R. niveus can be 
reclassified as R. delemar [7]. However, the currently outdated names of these species

are still used. For convenience, the names of the species as used in the cited papers are

Many different types of lipases have been identified and characterized from Rhizopus 
sp. (Table 1). Some Rhizopus lipases have been commercialized by various 
companies, including Amano, Sigma and Biocatalysts, among others, and the closely 
related Rhizomucor miehei lipase is manufactured by Novozymes (Table 2). They are 
widely employed in many industrial applications, including the bioenergy, 
pharmaceutical and food industries, particularly for lipid modification due to their 
high specificity for the sn-1,3-position [8]. 
  Decades ago, versatile lipases from Rhizopus sp. were reviewed by Haas [9] and 
Bornscheuer [10]. Since then, much progress has been made regarding these desirable 
Rhizopus lipases. New lipase genes and structures from Rhizopus sp. have been 
reported, and the heterologous expression of Rhizopus lipases has been established as 
a model system. The properties of Rhizopus lipases have been greatly improved by 
novel technologies of protein engineering. Furthermore, Rhizopus lipases also have 
been used in new applications for the production of renewable resources, biodiesel, 
and chiral organic compounds due to their high stability and activity in organic 
solvents. This review provides an overview of new approaches for enzyme 
characterization, genetics, structure, heterologous expression, bioengineering and 
other applications of Rhizopus lipases.

2. Multiplicity and Characterization of Rhizopus sp. Lipases 
  Rhizopus sp. strains can produce various isolipases. The multiplicity of lipase forms 
produced by Rhizopus strains is usually caused by post-translational modifications. 
Kohno et al. [11] reported two forms of lipases from R. niveus that were distinguished 
by the presence of a non-covalently linked small glycopeptide. Dobrev et al. [12] 
isolated three isolipases from R. arrhizus (Lip I, Lip II and Lip III) that differed in 
molecular weight (Lip I 80 kDa, Lip II 39.7 kDa and Lip III 6.9 kDa), degree of 
glycosylation (51.61% for Lip I, 74.17% for Lip II and 55.60% for Lip III) and 
enzymatic properties [12]. The results suggest that it is common for lipases from 
Rhizopus sp. to be glycosylated. Proteolytic cleavage during the post-translational 
process can also generate different types of lipases. Western blot analysis detected 
two forms of R. oryzae lipases (ROLs) with different molecular masses (34 kDa and 
31 kDa) localized in the supernatant (34 kDa and 31 kDa), membranes (31 kDa) and 
cell wall (34 kDa and 31 kDa). The 31-kDa lipase is obtained after the truncation of 
the N terminus of the 34-kDa protein [13].  
  Under varied culture conditions, Rhizopus sp. strains have been reported to produce 
different isolipases. For example, R. chinensis isolated from Da QU, which is 
employed for brewing traditional Chinese liquor, produces three forms of lipases (36 
kDa, 62 kDa and 33 kDa) by solid-state fermentation (SSF) [14, 15], but by 
submerged fermentation (SmF), this strain produces one identical 33-kDa lipase and 
two other lipase forms (39 kDa and 59 kDa) [16, 17]. Two extracellular lipases from 
R. homothallicus obtained from SSF and SmF have identical molecular weights and

  A summary of Rhizopus lipase properties is shown in Table 1. Because the 
enzymatic properties of a crude lipase could be easily affected by contaminated 
proteins and other compounds in an unpurified solution, only purified lipases are 
listed. As shown in Table 1, most Rhizopus lipases require a pH value between 6.0 and 
8.5 for optimal enzymatic activity and have an optimal temperature between 30°C and 
45°C. Rhizopus lipases show different chain length selectivity, but most preferentially 
hydrolyze esters with a fatty acid chain of C8~C18. The position specificity of lipases 
is an important characteristic that can be used to modify the composition of oils and 
fats to form structured triacylglycerols. Most lipases from Rhizopus sp. show a strong 
preference for the hydrolysis of ester bonds at the sn-1 and sn-3 positions of a 
triacylglycerol, such as those from R. oryzae [19, 20], R. delemar [21], and R. 
rhizopodiformis [20], whereas the lipase from R. homothallicus shows no positional 
specificity [18] and two intracellular lipases from R. chinensis display opposite 
positional specificity [16]. Rhizopus lipases also show remarkable stability in organic 
solvents [22, 23], resulting in improvements for synthesis reactions in organic 
solvents.

  Due to the activity of lipases at interfaces, interfacial phenomena have a detrimental 
influence on both enzymes and reactions. The binding of lipases at the water/lipid 
interface depends on the “interface quality”, which refers to the physico-chemistry, 
composition, and structure of the interface [24]. Emulsification of water-insoluble 
substrates requires a surfactant, such as a detergent, a polar lipid, bile salts, and so on. 
The effects of different surfactants on lipase activity have been widely investigated and 
summarized by Reis et al. [24]. Although a lipase can be denatured or activated under 
different conditions of interfacial tension or inhibited by certain surfactants, lipase 
activity as a function of the interfacial composition is more affected by substrate 
inaccessibility rather than enzyme denaturation or inactivation [24]. Olive oil has been 
commonly used as a natural substrate for the assay of the hydrolytic activity of lipases 
because it is easily obtainable, inexpensive and easy-to-use [25]. The acid liberated 
from olive oil hydrolysis can be assayed by titration. The sensitivity of this method is 
within 1 µmol of fatty acid released per min and is not reliable below an activity of 0.1 
μmol per min [26]. A higher sensitivity was obtained from a colorimetric method. The 
synthetic p-nitrophenyl derivatives of fatty acids (especially p-nitrophenyl palmitate 
and p-nitrophenyl laurate) are used as substrates and hydrolyzed to produce a yellow 
colored p-nitrophenol, which can be monitored continuously at a wavelength of 
approximately 410 nm. However, because the substrate is synthetic, the results should 
be confirmed using a natural substrate, such as olive oil [25]. Other lipase assay 
methods in addition to the most commonly used titrimetric and spectrophotometric 
methods include radiolabeling, fluorimetry, surface tension method, HPLC, GC, NMR

  Because lipases are very useful in organic synthesis, a synthetic assay was carried out 
to evaluate their performance in organic solvents. Esterification of a fatty acid with 
alcohol, for example, oleic acid with 1-heptanol or octoic acid with ethanol, was used 
for the measurement of the synthetic activity [28, 29]. The synthetic activity is usually 
calculated by monitoring the concentration of the product via GC or HPLC. 
Interestingly, the most active lipases in the synthetic reaction were not necessarily very 
active in the hydrolytic assay [28]. The membrane-bound lipase from R. chinensis also 
had a different optimum pH and temperature in aqueous and non-aqueous media [29].   
 
4. Rhizopus Lipase Genes 
  The genome sequence of R. delemar RA 99-880 was the first sequence of a 
Rhizopus species to be completed [30], and our lab then completed the genome 
sequence of R. chinensis CCTCC M201021 [31]. At present, several genomic projects 
involving Rhizopus sp. are in progress. Fifty three and 110 predicted lipase genes 
have been identified in the genomes of R. delemar RA 99-880 and R. chinensis 
CCTCC M201021, respectively. However, only few of these predicted lipase genes 
have been cloned and characterized. The lipase genes that have been characterized are 
listed in Table 3. Within the R. oryzae group, the lipase genes differed only in several 
amino acids or were completely identical [10]. According to sequence alignment

5. Structural Features  
 The crystal structures of R. niveus lipase (PDB ID: 1LGY, 2.20 Å), R. delemar 
lipase (PDB ID: 1TIC, 2.60 Å) and RCL (PDB ID: 4L3W, 2.00 Å) are available in the 
Protein Data Bank (PDB). The crystal structures of these lipases are highly similar 
due to the high identity of their primary structures (which is 100% between 1LGY and 
1TIC and 82.16% between 1LGY/1TIC and 4L3W) (Figure 2). Compared with 
lipases from other genera, these structures show the closest similarity to the structure 
of the R. miehei lipase (RML, PDB ID: 4TGL). These lipases all share an α/β 
hydrolase fold composed of nine α-helices and eight β-strands. The asymmetric unit 
of the 1TIC lipase comprises two molecules with disparate lid conformations [32] 
(Figure 2). The conformation of the lid in one molecule (molecule B) is closed, as 
expected, and thus blocks the active site, whereas that of a different molecule 
(molecule A) is in the intermediate position between the closed and open 
configuration due to the effect of the protein-detergent interaction with the crystal 
contacts [32]. Due to the absence of detergent in the crystal of 1LGY or 4L3W, the lid 
conformation matches that of the closed form of molecule B in 1TIC [33]. The lid of 
the closely related structure 4TGL complexed with an inhibitor adopts an open form

movement of the lid creates a large hydrophobic patch around the catalytic triad, 
yielding an ‘open’ conformation, which provides a structural basis for the well-known 
two-state model of interfacial activation [34, 35]. However, the semi-open lid 
conformation in 1TIC in the presence of a detergent calls the simplicity of the 
two-state model of interfacial activation into question [32]. In addition, the crystal

lid in an open conformation without a requirement for detergents, lipids or substrate 
analogues, which suggests that the lid can assume an open conformation in the 
absence of an oil-water interface [36]. Gonzalez-Navarro et al. [37] investigated the 
activation of four lipases from R. delemar, Candida rugosa, Geotrichum candidum 
and Humicola lanuginose and proposed a hypothetical model. According to the model, 
an equilibrium exists among lipase intermediates with closed and open conformations 
in aqueous solution, and this equilibrium can be modulated by the composition of the 
microenvironment. A systematic study based on a biophysical approach indicates that 
the interfacial microenvironment has a significant impact on lipase activation [24].

6. Protein Engineering 
  Molecular engineering technologies have been applied to better understand the 
catalytic mechanism or have been used in an effort to improve the specific properties 
of Rhizopus lipases. The key residues for enzyme function and substrate specificity

ACCEPTED MANUSCRIPT
 
13 
 
have been investigated using site-directed mutagenesis and have been reviewed by 
Pleiss et al. [38] and Bornscheuer [10]. Recently, new technologies, such as directed 
evolution, module recombination and saturation mutagenesis, have been applied to 
tailor the enzyme properties of Rhizopus lipases and are summarized in Table 4.  
  The lid domain has been used as the target for a rational design to alter the substrate 
specificity and thermostability of lipases. Upon lipase activation, the lid is open and 
several lid residues that are predicted to reside in the substrate-binding groove are 
exposed on the surface, indicating that engineering of the lid can alter lipase substrate 
selectivity. The lid of RCL was replaced by those from ROL, RML and ferulic acid 
esterase from Aspergillus niger (AnFaeA) to study the impact of the lid on the lipase 
chain length specificity [39, 40]. Replacement of the lid with that from ROL or RML 
did not markedly alter the chain length specificity of the chimeras, whereas replacing 
the hydrophobic lid from RCL with a hydrophilic lid from AnFaeA markedly 
modified the substrate specificity to adapt to hydrosoluble substrates. In consideration 
of the relationship between structure and function, the amphipathic nature of the lid is 
vital to substrate specificity. The lid domain is also the most flexible part of the lipase 
structure, which has caused interest in research regarding the balance between 
structural flexibility and molecular stability. The relationship between lipase activity 
and lid rigidity has been investigated via the rational design of an additional disulfide 
bond in the lid hinge of RCL [41]. The disulfide bridge generated between F95C and 
F214C improved the t1/2 value at 60°C by eleven-fold without compromising the 
catalytic rate, and this is the first study that found an improvement in lipase

  Rational design is usually restricted by the difficulty associated with predicting 
which amino acid mutation will lead to a specific enzyme property, even when 
high-resolution structural data have been gathered. In sharp contrast, directed 
evolution, which is a procedure that involves repeated mutation cycles and selecting 
mutants with desirable properties, is now well established. Shibamoto et al. [42] 
constructed a combinatorial yeast library by error-prone PCR via the cell-surface 
display of ROL and found clones with an altered lipase specificity for the hydrolysis 
or methanolysis of soybean oil. The optimal temperature of the R. niveus lipase was 
improved by 15°C via random mutagenesis [43]. The E218V mutation has been 
identified as being responsible for the change in the optimal temperature [43]. A 
desirable mutant of the R. arrhizus lipase with both improved thermostability and an 
increased optimal temperature has been selected using error-prone PCR and DNA 
shuffling methods [44]. Yu et al. [45] used in vivo recombination to establish a rapid, 
simplified and efficient strategy for the construction of a mutant gene library of P. 
pastoris. This method, combined with error-prone PCR and DNA shuffling, improved 
the Tm value of RCL by 22°C. In an effort to improve the stability of ROL for lipid 
oxidation products, such as aldehydes, six lysines and all of the histidine residues out 
of the 22 amino acid residues (15 lysines and 7 histidines) prone to react with 
aldehydes, except for the catalytic histidine, were selected and subjected to saturation 
mutagenesis [46]. The most stable mutant (H201S/K168I) showed an increased

7. Heterologous expression 
  Most Rhizopus lipases described in the literature are produced in very small 
amounts, which is not suitable for large-scale industrial application. Another 
drawback of working with native microorganisms is that Rhizopus sp. strains usually 
produce multiple isolipases with different biocatalytic properties, which complicates 
their biocatalytic application due to the existence of unwanted side effects caused by 
undesirable enzymes. Thus, to increase the potential industrial applications of these 
lipases, one of the most promising strategies is to clone the lipase genes and express 
them in a host microorganism, which minimizes the complexity of the bioprocess and 
reduces the production cost of large quantities lipases [47]. The production of 
Rhizopus lipases has been established as a model system to study heterologous 
expression systems in different hosts, such as Escherichia coli [48], Saccharomyces 
cerevisiae [49, 50] and Pichia pastoris [51, 52]. The expression of Rhizopus lipases in 
E. coli has achieved limited success and has been summarized by Bornscheuer [10]. 
Compared to prokaryotic expression systems, eukaryotic expression systems have the 
advantages of secretion into culture medium and avoidance of cell disruption and 
post-translational modifications, such as glycosylation and disulfide bond formation. 
Here we review the progress of the expression of Rhizopus lipases in yeast.

7.1 Heterologous expression in S. cerevisiae 
  All Rhizopus lipases deposited in GenBank (Table 3) are composed of a signal 
sequence, a prosequence and a mature sequence. The prosequence is important for the 
expression of Rhizopus lipases. The R. oryzae prolipase gene (ProROL) fused with the 
α-factor signal sequence has been expressed in S. cerevisiae [53]. Two forms of ROL, 
the full-length lipase ProROL (46 kDa) and mature lipase that contains 28 amino 
acids from the prosequence (r28ROL, 35 kDa), were secreted into culture medium. 
N-terminal amino acid sequence analysis revealed that the processed form r28ROL is 
cleaved by a Kex2-like protease in S. cerevisiae at the KR recognition site in the 
prosequence [53]. However, no lipase activity can be detected during the expression 
of the mature R. oryzae lipase (mROL) in S. cerevisiae [53, 54]. The effect of the 
prosequence in ROL has been investigated further. The activity of mROL was 
recovered through in trans co-expression of the prosequence [54, 55]. Via an analysis 
of the truncation of the ROL prosequence, which was co-expressed with mROL in 
trans, residues 20-37 in the prosequence were found to be necessary for secretion and 
residues 38-57 were found to be critical for the formation of the active ROL, which 
may function as an intramolecular chaperone [55]. Moreover, the Rhizopus sp. 
prolipases are more thermostable than truncated lipases [49, 56]. In addition to 
extracellular expression, ROL was also successfully displayed on the surface of S. 
cerevisiae and had an activity of 350.6 U/L [57-59].

  Differently than in the S. cerevisiae expression system, the expression of the 
prolipase gene from R. arrhizus in P. pastoris resulted in the detection of only a 
truncated lipase in the medium. Full-length prolipase could not be detected in the 
medium, which may indicate that the activity of the Kex2-like protease is higher in P. 
pastoris than in S. cerevisiae [60]. Two forms of lipases were produced by the 
expression of the prolipase gene from R. chinensis in P. pastors; the prosequence 
truncated lipase (r27RCL) and the mature lipase (mRCL) [51], which was likely 
processed by serine proteases in culture medium. It seemed that the prosequence from 
RCL is more efficient than that from ROL for facilitating the secretion of a functional 
lipase [61]. The substitution of the prosequence of ROL by that from RCL resulted in 
a chimeric lipase activity (4050 U/mL) in P. pastoris that was 11-fold higher than that 
of ROL [61]. Glycosylation engineering was employed to show that the N-glycan on 
the prosequence is very important for the expression and secretion of RCL [62].  
  The activity of mROL expressed in S. cerevisiae was not detectable [53, 54], 
whereas mROL was functionally expressed and secreted in P. pastoris [63, 64]. The 
expression of mROL was compared for different inducer and constitutive promoters 
[65, 66], i.e., the glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase promoter (PGAP), the 
alcohol oxidase 1 promoter (PAOX) and the formaldehyde dehydrogenase 1 promoter 
(PFLD1). Under the constitutive PGAP promoter, the extracellular expression of 
mROL was very low [66]. PAOX can be greatly induced in the presence of methanol 
but tightly repressed in the presence of many common carbon sources, such as 
glucose and glycerol, but PFLD1 is induced by methylamine, a less flammable and

volatile inducer in methanol-free medium. Valero’s group [65, 67] reported the 
successful expression of mROL in P. pastoris under the PFLD1 promoter using 
methylamine as the nitrogen source and sorbitol as the carbon source. Productivity 
under the PFLD1 promoter was comparable to that obtained with the classic PAOX 
system [65, 67]. More efficient fermentation strategies using the PFLD1 promoter 
should result if more knowledge regarding methylamine metabolism in P. pastoris is 
acquired. At present, PAOX remains the most used promoter for the expression of 
Rhizopus lipases [52, 68-72]. 
  Studies that aimed to augment the production of foreign proteins in P. pastoris have 
found that the gene dosage of a preferred expression cassette is a significant factor 
[70]. Optimization of the lipase gene dosage greatly improved RCL expression in P. 
pastoris [68]. Of strains with one, three, five and six copies of the lipase gene, a 
maximum lipase activity of 12,500 U/mL was obtained in the five-copy strain, and 
this activity was 6.2-fold higher than that obtained in the one-copy strain [68]. In 
some cases, increasing the gene copy number resulted in a reduction in the final 
productivity [68] or a had a negative effect on cell growth [70], which indicates that 
the overexpression of lipase stresses P. pastoris cells. Transcriptomic studies have 
shown that the heterologous overexpression of Rhizopus lipases in P. pastoris indeed 
triggers the unfolded protein response [68, 73]. The co-expression of chaperons can 
relieve cellular stress caused by the overexpression of foreign proteins. ERO1p and 
PDI are two ER-associated chaperones that are involved in protein folding [74]. 
Co-expression with these two chaperons greatly improved the productivity of RCL in

  The Mut phenotype should also be taken into account for the optimization of gene 
expression. The expression of a single-copy mROL in P. pastoris under the control of

8. Biotechnological Applications 
  Lipases specific for the sn-1,3-position are particularly useful for the production of 
structured triacylglycerols [25]. Most Rhizopus lipases exhibit high sn-1,3-positional 
specificity. Since these Rhizopus lipases were discovered in the middle of the 
twentieth century, they have been most commonly used for lipid modification or 
triacylglycerol hydrolysis to produce structured lipids as well as mono- and 
diglycerides [9, 10]. Recently, Rhizopus lipases have shown promise in applications 
for the production of biodiesel and chiral compounds. In this review, the progress 
using Rhizopus lipases in the areas of bioenergy and pharmaceuticals is also 
discussed.  
 
8.1. Production of structured triacylglycerols 
  Rhizopus lipases have been successfully applied in the synthesis of MLM 
triacylglycerols, human milk fat substitutes (HMFS), cocoa butter replacements or 
oils with a specific structure. Table 5 lists the recent progress in the production of 
structured triacylglycerols catalyzed by Rhizopus lipases. The production of 
low-caloric of MLM triacylglycerols, which are characterized by medium-chain fatty 
acids at the sn-1 and sn-3 position, and a long-chain fatty acid at the sn-2 position, 
was catalyzed by an immobilized ROL via the acidolysis of olive oil with caprylic or 
capric acid [87-89]. A cocoa butter-like fat was produced by the acidolysis of 
sunflower oil with stearic or palmitic acid using an immobilized ROL [90]. The 
reaction kinetics were studied, and the established model well-predicted the final

has received considerable attention during the past decades. The enzymatic 
production of biodiesel using lipases as catalysts is an environmentally friendly 
approach that offers several advantages, such as avoidance of side reactions, high 
specificity and mild reaction conditions [26, 97]. This section describes biodiesel 
production by Rhizopus lipases. For biodiesel production, ROLs are the most often

9. Conclusions 
  Lipases from Rhizopus species have been investigated in depth and are very 
promising for various applications. However, the following three aspects still require 
further study. First, the N-terminal sequencing of purified lipases from 
lipase-producing Rhizopus cells revealed that different types of lipase genes exist in

Rhizopus sp. (Table 1). In addition, the genome sequencing of Rhizopus sp. has 
revealed hundreds of predicted lipases. However, to date, only a limited number of 
Rhizopus lipase gene types have been cloned and expressed. Thus, extensive efforts 
are required to discover more versatile Rhizopus lipase genes to further the 
development of these desirable catalysts. Second, protein engineering has and will 
continue to lead to changes in new and remarkable characteristics for specific 
applications and deepen our understanding of the mechanisms underlying lipase 
activity. Third, although the enantioselective resolution of many different types of 
substrates has been achieved with Rhizopus lipases, the molecular basis of the 
enantioselectivity toward chiral esters remains unexplored. Further investigations are 
required to achieve new insights into the structural basis of Rhizopus lipases to 
provide theoretical procedures for the rational design of their enantioselectivity to 
improve application. Along with an in-depth investigation of Rhizopus lipases, an 
increasing number of different types of lipases with more desirable functions will be 
discovered, and the range of their applications will become wider.
